title: I built an attention guardian system to catch my own distractions. It worked too well.
content:
I built an attention guardian system to catch my own distractions. It worked too well.

---

Three weeks ago, I made a decision that scared me: I installed a keystroke and mouse tracking system on my own computer. Not for work. Not for my team. For myself.

I wanted to know: where does my attention actually go? Not where I think it goes. Where it really goes.

**The Setup**
I wrote a simple Python script that logged every app switch, every Alt+Tab, every mouse movement. Every 30 seconds, it captured the active window title. I ran this for 21 days. Across 147 working hours.
The results werent what I expected.

**The Data**

- Total app switches: 4,892
- Average switches per hour: 33.3
- Maximum switches in a single hour: 87
- Time between switches when focused: 4.2 minutes (on average)
- My claimed deep work sessions: 2.1 hours
- Actual deep work within those sessions: 47 minutes

I was lying to myself. Systematically. Mathematically. Quantifiably lying.

**The Pattern**
The guardian system caught 312 distinct attention leaks - moments where I switched context without conscious decision. Most happened at predictable times:
- 10:47 AM (right after standup)
- 2:33 PM (post-lunch crash)
- 5:12 PM (end of day rush)
But the worst part: 67% of my quick checks turned into 15+ minute sessions. The quick Slack check that became a 23-minute thread. The 2-minute email check that became a strategy discussion.

**The Intervention**
Week 2, I added a rule: when the system detected 3 consecutive app switches, it would display a full-screen prompt: What are you running from?
Cringe? Yes. Effective? Surprisingly yes.
It broke the loop 41% of the time. Those 41% became my most productive hours.

**What I Learned**
The biggest insight was not about productivity. It was about avoidance. I was not distracted - I was escaping. Every context switch had an emotional signature. The code captured the what. The system could not capture the why.
But now I know: I do not have an attention problem. I have an avoidance problem. And there is a system catching me every time I try to escape.

**The Cost**
21 days of data collection. 4,892 moments of self-revelation. 312 attention leaks finally seen.
And one uncomfortable truth: I am my own worst security threat.

---
Has anyone else tracked their own attention like this? What patterns did you find? Or are you too scared to look?
